lead: An aircraft generator is useless until its voltage is held steady, its output is switched onto a busbar, and its faults are cleared before wiring overheats. Follow one generator channel from the engine shaft to the loads. It covers DC generation with shunt and compound machines, AC generation at 115 V 400 Hz from an integrated drive generator and at 360-800 Hz variable frequency, and the 28 V and 270 V DC systems built on them. The chain is simple; the protection is what makes it safe.
prereq: You need: first-year DC and AC circuit theory — Ohm's law, three-phase power and power factor — and 3.9 shows how the field current is actually controlled.

sections.h3: The DC channel: generator, cut-out, bus, with the regulator as control

blocks.text: Every load draws from a busbar, not directly from a generator. A generator converts engine shaft power into electrical power. Its voltage must stay inside a band because lamps, radios and instruments are designed for that band. One source of 28 V DC is a shunt or compound DC generator. A shunt generator has its field winding across the armature; output voltage rises with speed and field current. A compound generator adds a series field that lifts voltage as load current rises, so the regulator has less work to do. The regulator is covered in 3.9.

The power path in a DC channel is: generator → reverse-current cut-out → busbar → loads. The reverse-current cut-out is a contactor that closes when generator voltage is above bus voltage. It opens when current tries to flow from the battery back into the generator. Without it, a stopped generator becomes a motor and drains the battery. This is a DC device, not an AC generator circuit breaker.

The voltage regulator is not in that power path. It is a control block: it senses bus voltage and controls the generator field current. It carries no load current, so it is drawn beside the generator, not between the generator and the busbar. How it senses and controls is in 3.9.

28 V DC is the long-standing low-voltage standard. 270 V DC appears where high-power DC loads make lower voltage wasteful; it is not a scaled 28 V system, because higher voltage changes insulation and arc behaviour.

sections.h3: AC generation: constant frequency and variable frequency

blocks.text: An AC generator's frequency follows its speed: f = p × n ÷ 120. Here f is frequency in hertz, p is the number of poles and n is speed in revolutions per minute. A four-pole machine at 12 000 rpm gives 400 Hz. Engine speed is not constant, so a 400 Hz supply needs a constant-speed drive. An integrated drive generator (IDG) puts that drive and an oil-cooled generator in one unit. It produces 115 V AC at 400 Hz. The generator control unit (GCU) is a control block: it regulates voltage by controlling field current and it protects the generator. The generator circuit breaker (GCB) is the switch that connects the generator to the AC bus. A transformer rectifier unit (TRU) then feeds the 28 V DC bus; TRUs are in 3.2.

Variable-frequency (VF) generation avoids the constant-speed drive. The generator runs at engine gearbox speed and its output varies from 360 Hz to 800 Hz. Loads are designed to accept that range or to rectify it first. VF saves weight and maintenance. Newer architectures use 235 V AC VF and 270 V DC; the A320 and B787 comparison is in 3.12.

The AC power path is: generator → GCB → AC bus → loads, with a TRU branch from the AC bus to the DC bus. The GCU sits outside this path. It senses generator voltage, current, frequency and field current, controls the field, and commands the GCB to trip or the drive to disconnect.
Protection removes a fault before it damages wiring or the generator. The action matters as much as the name.

head: Protection
What it protects
Typical action
rows: GCU removes field and trips GCB
Reduce field; trip if it persists
Mechanical disconnect, not an electrical trip

blocks.text: A differential fault compares currents at the two ends of a winding; a difference means current is escaping through a fault. An earth fault detects current returning through the airframe. Both act fast. Over-excitation is different: the GCU first reduces field current, because tripping the GCB alone does not remove the field. A seized IDG drive is handled by the drive disconnect, a mechanical action. So 'the contactor opens for every fault' is wrong.

examples.question: A twin-engine aircraft has two 28 V DC generators, each rated 200 A continuous. Non-essential loads draw 180 A and essential loads draw 60 A. One generator fails. (a) How much load must be shed so the surviving generator is not overloaded? (b) If all non-essential loads are dropped, what load does the surviving generator carry, and what fraction of its rating is that?
steps: Total load before failure = non-essential + essential = 180 A + 60 A = 240 A.
Minimum load to shed = 240 A − 200 A = 40 A.
Dropping all non-essential load removes 180 A.
Remaining load = 240 A − 180 A = 60 A, which is the essential load.
examples.answer: At least 40 A must be shed; after all non-essential load is dropped the survivor carries 60 A, which is 30% of its 200 A rating.
examples.check:
non_essential = 180.0
essential = 60.0
rating = 200.0
total = non_essential + essential
shed = total - rating
survivor = total - non_essential
percent = 100.0 * survivor / rating
print(shed)
print(survivor)
print(percent)

traps: The GCB does not open for every fault. Over-excitation is first corrected by reducing field current; a seized IDG drive is cleared by the drive disconnect, a mechanical action.
400 Hz from an IDG is constant frequency because a constant-speed drive holds generator speed. A 360-800 Hz variable-frequency supply is not a faulty 400 Hz supply; the range is its design.
Reverse-current cut-out is a DC device that stops the battery driving the generator as a motor. It is not the AC generator circuit breaker.
GCU and GCB are different: the GCU senses, regulates and decides; the GCB carries and breaks generator current.
Shedding exactly the calculated deficit may not match the load blocks available. Dropping a 180 A non-essential bus leaves 60 A on the survivor; state the block actually dropped.

quiz.q: In a typical 28 V DC channel, list the power blocks after the generator in order up to the loads, and name the control block that is not in the power path.
quiz.a: Power blocks: reverse-current cut-out → busbar → loads. The voltage regulator is the control block; it senses bus voltage and controls field current, and it carries no load current.

quiz.q: What does a generator control unit (GCU) do?
quiz.a: It regulates generator voltage by controlling field current and protects by sensing voltage, current, frequency and field current, then commanding GCB trip or drive disconnect.

quiz.q: Why does a 400 Hz AC generator need a constant-speed drive?
quiz.a: Frequency is f = p × n ÷ 120, so it follows generator speed. Engine speed varies, so a constant-speed drive holds the speed that gives 400 Hz.

quiz.q: Why is a reverse-current cut-out not the same as an AC generator circuit breaker?
quiz.a: The cut-out is a DC contactor that opens when battery current flows back into a generator. The AC GCB is a three-phase contactor controlled by the GCU for generator faults and bus connection.

quiz.q: Two 150 A, 28 V DC generators supply a total load of 170 A, made of 120 A non-essential and 50 A essential. One generator fails. How much load must be shed, and what does the survivor carry after all non-essential load is dropped?
quiz.a: Total = 170 A; one generator gives 150 A; shed at least 20 A. Dropping 120 A leaves 50 A on the survivor, which is 50 ÷ 150 = 33.3% of rating.

quiz.q: A GCU trips the GCB on differential protection but only reduces field on over-excitation. Explain why both actions are correct.
quiz.a: Differential protection detects current escaping through an internal or earth fault, so the generator must be isolated from the bus. Over-excitation is excessive field current; tripping the GCB does not remove field, so the GCU first reduces field and trips only if it persists.

quiz.q: An aircraft has a 115 V AC 400 Hz bus and a 270 V DC bus. Explain why protection settings for the 270 V DC bus cannot simply be copied from a 28 V DC bus.
quiz.a: At 270 V DC the current for the same power is lower, but the higher voltage sustains arcs and stresses insulation. Clearance, arc suppression and trip times differ; protection is designed for the higher voltage, not scaled from 28 V.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern transport aircraft are moving toward higher-voltage DC and variable-frequency AC to save weight and maintenance. The search terms are 'more-electric aircraft', '270 V DC', 'variable-frequency generation' and 'generator control unit'. The next design question is how protection changes when a bus can be fed from several sources.
